strengths: Addresses a novel and underexplored security problem: action-level backdoor attacks specifically against Trajectory Optimization (TO) models such as Decision Transformer, GDT, and Decision ConvFormer, which differ fundamentally from reward-based RL agents.

The paper conducts a systematic empirical investigation (Section 3) into the roles of target action selection, trigger design, and reward manipulation before proposing the method, providing useful insights (e.g., reward manipulation is ineffective for TO models, boundary target actions are much easier to attack than interior ones) that motivate the design choices.

Extensive experimentation across 6 D4RL environments (locomotion, navigation, manipulation), 3 TO model architectures, and 3 diverse target action types, with results averaged over multiple seeds, giving a fairly comprehensive evaluation.

TrojanTO achieves substantially better attack effectiveness (ASR) and stealth (BTP) than two adapted baselines (Baffle, IMC) while requiring a much smaller poisoning budget (0.3% vs 10%), and the CP metric appropriately balances effectiveness and stealth.

Thorough ablation studies (component-level, alternating frequency, data-selection method, attack budget) and additional robustness experiments (persistent backdoors, trigger perturbations) strengthen the empirical support for the claims.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, algorithm pseudocode, and extensive appendix material.
Honest limitations section acknowledging lack of automated methods for trigger-dimension/target-action selection and absence of effective defenses.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination/adaptation of existing techniques (IMC-style bi-level trigger-model co-optimization, MI-FGSM trigger optimization, standard data filtering) to a new setting rather than a fundamentally new attack paradigm; the individual components (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning) are relatively simple engineering heuristics.

Performance is highly inconsistent across environments/models (e.g., DT on Ant CP=0.302, DC on Pen CP=0.477, DT on Hopp CP=0.365), which somewhat undermines the claim of 'consistent robustness across tasks and architectures'; some BTP values exceed 1.0 (e.g., GDT Walk 1.089) without explanation, raising questions about evaluation stability.

Trigger dimension selection is shown to be brittle and highly sensitive (Table 2, ASR ranging from ~0.9 to 0.0 depending on dimensions), and the paper admits no principled method exists for selecting effective dimensions, relying on manual/random search — this limits the generality and real-world applicability of the attack.
The threshold ε used for defining a 'successful' attack in the ASR metric is not explicitly specified in the main text, making it hard to judge how strict/lenient the success criterion is.

No defense or detection experiments are included; the paper only briefly notes that an existing reward-based defense is ineffective, but does not explore or propose any mitigation, limiting the completeness of the security analysis.

The real-world significance/motivation for backdooring offline RL/TO models is somewhat abstract; concrete deployment scenarios and consequences (beyond illustrative examples in the appendix) are not deeply analyzed.

Some results (e.g., Table 14 trajectory poisoning ablation) show baseline trajectory-poisoning methods can achieve very high performance at certain poisoning rates comparable to TrojanTO, suggesting the marginal benefit of the proposed batch-poisoning trick over simpler alternatives may be less than claimed in some settings.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: security vulnerabilities of Trajectory Optimization (TO) models (DT/GDT/DC) to backdoor attacks, which differ mechanistically from prior RL backdoor work (reward-based vs. sequence modeling).

The paper performs a useful preliminary empirical study (Section 3) isolating the effects of target action selection, trigger dimension/value choice, and reward manipulation before designing the attack, which is a sensible and informative methodology.

Extensive experimental coverage: 6 D4RL environments, 3 TO architectures, 3 distinct target action types, 3 random seeds, with well-defined metrics (ASR, BTP, CP) and thorough ablations (component-level, alternation frequency, data selection, attack budget).

TrojanTO achieves a notably lower poisoning rate (0.3%) than baselines while generally improving CP, and the paper includes reasonably transparent implementation and hyperparameter details in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core techniques (MI-FGSM trigger optimization, bi-level/alternating trigger-model co-optimization borrowed from IMC, simple length-based trajectory filtering, and single-transition batch poisoning) are largely adaptations of existing methods rather than fundamentally new contributions; the main claimed novelty is the application domain rather than the method itself.

Trigger dimension selection remains ad hoc and unprincipled — the paper explicitly acknowledges (Appendix F) that gradient-based/Grad-CAM/NTK-based selection methods show no correlation with attack efficacy, and the reported best dimensions (1,2,3) appear to be found by brute-force search without a generalizable rationale, undermining the practical applicability and scientific rigor of the trigger design.

Performance is highly inconsistent across target action types: CP averages 0.942 for target '1' but drops sharply to 0.536 for 'arithmetic' and 0.624 for 'fixed random', with some cells (e.g., DT/Hopp arithmetic CP=0.039, DT/Pen fixed-random ASR=0), suggesting the method is far less robust than the aggregate averages in the main table imply.

No defense or detection evaluation is provided despite backdoor security being a paper's central concern; the limitations section merely states that an existing reward-based defense is 'often ineffective' without any empirical analysis of alternative detection/mitigation strategies, leaving the security implications only half-explored.

The threat model assumes an adversary can both control training and reliably inject precise, high-dimensional continuous perturbations into deployed state observations at inference time, which is a fairly strong and somewhat under-motivated real-world assumption; no real-world/physical robotic experiments are conducted to validate practical severity.

Baseline comparisons (Baffle, IMC) are adapted from different attack settings (online RL and adversarial-example/model-editing literature respectively) and may not represent strong, fairly-tuned baselines for the TO backdoor setting, raising questions about how much of TrojanTO's improvement stems from genuinely new insight versus baseline under-optimization.

Some result cells show TrojanTO performing worse than baselines (e.g., DT/Kit CP 0.614 vs Baffle 0.766, DC/Ant CP 0.559 vs IMC 0.752, DC/Pen CP 0.477 vs IMC 0.655), which are not discussed, leaving open questions about when/why the method underperforms.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: first work (to the authors' knowledge) to systematically investigate action-level backdoor attacks against Trajectory Optimization (TO) models, an increasingly popular class of offline RL models.

The paper follows a principled scientific approach: it first conducts targeted empirical studies (Section 3) to establish which factors (target action, trigger dimension/value, reward manipulation) actually matter for TO backdoors before designing the method, which strengthens the motivation for the proposed components.

Extensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse D4RL environments (locomotion, navigation, manipulation) and 3 distinct TO architectures (DT, GDT, DC), with results averaged over multiple seeds and multiple target action types, giving a fairly comprehensive picture of the method's generality.

Strong empirical results: TrojanTO clearly outperforms the Baffle and IMC baselines in the combined CP metric while using a much lower poisoning budget (0.3% vs. 10% for Baffle), and BTP is well preserved.

Thorough ablation studies (component-level, alternating frequency, data selection method, attack budget sensitivity for both TrojanTO and Baffle) that help isolate the contribution of trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, and alternating training.
Additional robustness analyses (persistent backdoor over multiple steps, robustness to trigger perturbation/noise) add useful depth beyond the core ASR/BTP/CP evaluation.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, and extensive appendix documenting implementation choices for each sub-experiment.
Honest discussion of limitations (no automated trigger-dimension selection, no effective defense, need for fine-tuning) in Appendix A, which is good scientific practice for a security paper.
weaknesses: Missing direct comparison to UniDoor [10], which is described in the related work as 'a universal framework for action-level backdoor attacks in deep RL' and appears to be the most closely related prior work; its absence from the experimental baselines (only Baffle and IMC are compared) leaves the relative advantage over the most relevant competitor unclear.

The individual technical components (MI-FGSM-based trigger optimization borrowed directly from adversarial example literature, IMC-inspired bi-level alternating optimization, simple length-based trajectory filtering, single-transition batch poisoning) are largely adaptations of existing techniques rather than fundamentally new algorithmic contributions; novelty lies mainly in problem formulation and combination rather than in new methodology.

No detection or defense evaluation is provided; while the paper acknowledges existing reward-based defenses are ineffective, it does not attempt any mitigation strategy or discuss how practitioners might detect such backdoors, which weakens the practical contribution of a security paper.

The trigger-dimension selection problem remains largely unresolved: the paper shows large variance in ASR depending on manually chosen dimensions and reports that gradient-based (Grad-CAM, NTK spectrum) selection methods do not correlate with effectiveness, meaning the practical attack still relies on brute-force search over dimension triplets, which limits real-world applicability and is only mentioned as future work.

Claims of 'broad applicability' and 'scalability across diverse TO model architectures' are based on only three transformer-style TO variants (DT, GDT, DC) that share substantial architectural similarity, so the generalization claim may be somewhat overstated relative to the diversity of models actually tested.

The threat model requires the adversary to have control over the training/post-training process (white-box access to fine-tune the released model), which, while standard in the backdoor literature, somewhat limits the paper's real-world threat significance compared to more restrictive data-poisoning-only threat models.

Some ablation results show non-trivial cross-environment variance and occasional counterintuitive patterns (e.g., CP collapsing to 0 for some Baffle/IMC settings, or BP ablation causing DC's ASR to drop drastically to 0.312 while GDT's only drops mildly), which are not deeply analyzed or explained beyond the aggregate statistics.

strengths: Addresses a novel and timely threat model: post-training, action-level backdoor attacks specifically tailored to Trajectory Optimization (TO) models (DT, GDT, DC), which differ fundamentally from classic Bellman-based RL agents that prior backdoor literature targeted.

Section 4's systematic empirical study of the three factors (target action, trigger design, reward manipulation) provides useful and non-obvious insights, e.g., that reward manipulation—central to prior RL backdoors—is largely ineffective for TO models, motivating the proposed design choices.

Extensive experimental evaluation: 6 D4RL environments spanning locomotion, navigation, and manipulation, 3 TO architectures, 3 distinct target action types, and 3 random seeds, with clear, well-defined metrics (ASR, BTP, CP).
Strong efficiency/stealth story: achieves substantially higher CP than Baffle and IMC baselines while using an extremely low poisoning budget (~0.3% of trajectories vs. Baffle's 10%).

Thorough ablations (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, alternating training; frequency of alternation; batch poisoning formulation; data selection quality; attack budget scaling) that support the necessity of each component.

Goes beyond basic attack demonstration to explore persistent backdoors, robustness to trigger perturbation, and multiple candidate defenses (pruning, provable defense, spectral analysis, activation clustering, fine-tuning), giving a fairly complete picture of the threat and possible mitigations.
Good reproducibility support: code released, detailed hyperparameters and dataset/task descriptions in the appendix.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core building blocks (MI-FGSM trigger optimization, IMC-style bi-level trigger/model co-optimization, standard notions of batch/data poisoning) are adapted from existing adversarial ML/backdoor literature rather than fundamentally new; the contribution is largely a careful engineering combination for a new setting.

Baselines (Baffle, IMC) were not originally designed for this exact post-training, low-budget TO setting, raising some concern about how tuned/fair these comparisons are, even though the paper attempts adaptation.

The ASR metric requires all action dimensions to simultaneously fall within a threshold of the target action; for high-dimensional action spaces (e.g., Pen with 24 dims) this is a very strict criterion whose sensitivity to the choice of ε is not analyzed.

Trigger dimension selection is largely ad hoc/brute-force search over small dimension subsets (Table 2, Appendix F); the paper itself acknowledges (Limitations) that no principled or automated method for dimension selection was found (even gradient/NTK-based attempts failed), which weakens the practical applicability of the attack.

Performance is notably inconsistent across environments/models (e.g., DC on Ant has much lower CP than on Half/Walk; DT on Hopp shows relatively low CP in Table 4), and this variability is not deeply analyzed or explained.

Some auxiliary studies (persistent backdoor, trigger perturbation robustness) are only conducted on 3 of the 6 environments (Hopp, Half, Walk), leaving generalization to navigation/manipulation tasks (Ant, Kit, Pen) for these properties untested.

The reward-manipulation-is-negligible claim (Section 4.3) is based on plots with quite large variance/noisy trends for some models (e.g., DT in Figure 1/7), making the conclusion somewhat less clean than stated.

Fine-tuning is shown to be a fairly effective defense (near-zero ASR with only 10% of original training steps), which somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of the attack as a serious, hard-to-mitigate real-world supply-chain threat.
